The materialism of the revolutionary democrats contained elements of a dialectical view of the world.
It expressed, above all, the ideology of revolutionary peasant forces.
D — Dialectical materialism: Historically, this is the most recent form of materialism up to our own stage.
It is Marxist materialism, expressing the ideology of the proletariat—the class whose historical task is the revolutionary transformation of the world.
We should add that this classification of the historical forms of materialism is neither final nor complete.
First, our knowledge of all its forms is still incomplete.
Second, some forms never developed into fully clear and independent systems, but remained at an early or embryonic stage.
For example, we did not include the forms of materialism that existed during the Middle Ages in the classification above.
In medieval Europe, the conflict between materialism and idealism appeared mainly in the struggle between nominalism (Nominalisme) and realism (Réalisme).
Neither the materialist nor the idealist side developed into a form clear enough to be separated out as one of the major historical categories listed above.

This is why the German historian of materialism Friedrich Albert Lange argued that medieval materialists became extremely skilled at hiding their real ideas. They developed materialism and atheism within works that, outwardly, appeared to defend God, religion, and theology.
Materialism within Arab-Islamic philosophy resembles medieval European materialism in this respect.
It too often appeared in unclear forms hidden within Islamic theological writing.

This made it easier for historians and researchers of Arab-Islamic philosophy—Arab, Muslim, and Orientalist alike—to find “justifications” for suppressing it, ignoring it, or distorting whatever signs of it did become visible.
One of the tasks of this book must therefore be to identify the forms taken by materialism within our philosophical heritage, as well as to uncover its materialist elements.
In doing so, we must try, if possible, to give a decisive answer to an important question.
By what standard should these forms be judged?
Should we measure them against the forms of materialism found in our own age—the age of dialectical materialism?
Should we compare them with the materialism of ancient Greece, with its forms of naive materialism?
Or should we judge them according to the age of al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, and Ibn Rushd?
And if so, what is the proper standard for their age?
To begin answering this question, we had to rely on the three principles mentioned earlier (pp. 40–41), because they follow from the requirements of the method we are using.
Along with the basic position toward the material world shared by the different forms of materialism, we must consider two other things.
First, we must examine the relationship between the materialist tendencies in our heritage and the social order that is reflected in them in one form or another.
Second, we must examine their relationship with the level reached by the natural sciences during the same historical period in which that heritage developed.

Once we accept these principles—especially the last two—we have to reject any attempt to judge the forms of materialism in our philosophical heritage by the standard of modern dialectical materialism, by the standard of ancient Greek materialism, or by any other standard disconnected from the social order within which Arab-Islamic philosophy developed.
The same applies to any standard disconnected from the level reached by the natural sciences during the age of that philosophy and that social order.
Why must we connect philosophy with the social order of its time?

Because philosophy is a particular form of social consciousness, and the way a particular society organizes material production plays the basic role in shaping the distinctive features of that form of consciousness.
Why must we also connect philosophy with the development of the natural sciences?
Because the development of philosophy in a materialist direction depends on the progress made by scientific knowledge of nature and on the extent to which science discovers nature’s objective laws.

The history of human knowledge in every age, as well as the reality of our own civilization, confirms that scientific knowledge of nature forms part of the foundation of every major advance in the different branches of knowledge—especially philosophy, with its attempt to understand the universe, nature, and society.
This point also has a social foundation.
Human knowledge of nature is directly connected with the material world outside us. It is therefore necessarily connected with material and social activity.
Indeed, the history of human civilizations shows in practical terms that this connection has always existed.
Human material needs have continually driven people, through the process of producing what they need, to discover the laws of nature and use those laws in production.
At the same time, the development of society’s material production and the development of the natural sciences have continually influenced one another.
The point can be put simply.

Just as the development of material production helps determine the development of human consciousness, of which philosophy is one of the highest forms, the development of the natural sciences also helps determine the forms that this consciousness takes.

The discussion so far has shown that the particular historical setting is what determines the forms taken by the materialist tendencies in the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage. What, then, shaped this historical setting?

First, there was the nature of the feudal mode of production in Arab-Islamic society during the Abbasid period. It existed alongside the remains of a declining slave system, a growing commercial sector, and relatively advanced craft industries.
Second, the natural sciences flourished during this period, especially in the fourth century AH, or the tenth century CE.

These two main factors help explain why the materialist tendencies in this philosophical heritage did not take one fixed form. Instead, they moved back and forth between metaphysical and dialectical forms, at a level suited to the historical conditions of the time.

There were two reasons for this movement. On the one hand, the philosophers themselves often shifted between different positions. On the other, metaphysical and dialectical tendencies were also mixed together within the natural sciences of the period.
The dialectical form appears most clearly when texts from this heritage discuss motion, time, and space, especially their relationship to matter.

This is one example of how philosophical ideas developed alongside the natural sciences. Studies of motion in nature, in particular, had made noticeable progress by this period. That progress found its way into philosophy partly because the philosophers themselves were often active in both fields. They combined philosophical thought with theoretical and experimental work on nature.

We can see the same movement between early metaphysical forms of materialism and early dialectical forms in Ibn Sīnā’s treatment of the relationship between the universal and the particular. He discusses this both as a question about existence in nature and as a question of logic.
For Ibn Sīnā, the relationship can take three forms:
The universal, or essence, can exist within the particular thing. This is the position we later find in Hegel. Aristotle’s view also appears in this form, and it contains the idea of immanence.
The universal can exist before individual things exist. This is the Platonic idealist position.
The universal can exist after individual things exist. This is the materialist position.
All three tendencies appeared in medieval scholastic philosophy: the Aristotelian, the Platonic, and the materialist.
It is worth noting here that materialist tendencies appeared in both Arab-Islamic philosophy and European scholastic philosophy before the rise of the mechanistic materialists.

So on this question we can see Ibn Sīnā moving between three positions: a metaphysical position, a purely idealist position, and a materialist position that contains, to some extent, a dialectical element. In the last of these, the universal gains its existence from the existence of particular things.

We said that the historical setting of a philosophical heritage is shaped mainly by the two factors just discussed. But these are not the only factors. To claim that they were would itself go against our scientific method.

We therefore have to consider other influences when defining the historical setting of any philosophical heritage. The Arab-Islamic heritage is no exception. In fact, we will see that these other influences played such a strong role in it that they became part of its historical character.
Some of these factors belong to the objective forces that guide the development and history of philosophy. Two are especially important.
First: the relationship between internal and external conditions

Every society has its own internal conditions: national, regional, and local. But it also exists within wider conditions beyond itself: international conditions, continental conditions, and the conditions of a larger region containing several societies that may resemble one another in important ways.
The relationship between these internal and external conditions, and the forms of social consciousness that grow out of it, necessarily affects the direction and form of philosophical development.
This means that philosophy does not develop only because of conditions inside one particular society. It is also influenced by conditions outside it.
This external factor is very important if we want to study an intellectual heritage—and especially a philosophical heritage—in a scientific and genuinely comprehensive way.
It is also important because it helps us reject a claim often found in bourgeois histories of philosophy: the idea of “closed civilizations” or “closed cultures.”

According to this view, a civilization or culture develops entirely within the local conditions of one people, nation, or region, without being influenced by other civilizations and without influencing them in return. We find versions of this idea in thinkers such as Spengler and Toynbee.
But this claim lacks historical support.

History does not give us examples of civilizations or cultures that were completely closed in this way. Could the idea really be applied to Chinese civilization? To Indian civilization? To Arab civilization?
A culture can certainly be relatively closed for a limited period. But at other stages it may be influenced by other cultures, may influence them, or may do both at once.

Arab culture is a clear example. It absorbed influences from several major civilizations and cultures, including Indian, Persian, and Greek culture. It later influenced European civilization and culture, and in modern times it came under European influence in return.
The same basic pattern can be found in the history of other civilizations and cultures.
We may even question whether it is always correct to speak of separate “civilizations” in the plural.

Humanity has, in one sense, a shared civilization. Its many elements were created by different peoples, nations, and human groups across the different stages of history. They developed through interaction that was sometimes continuous and sometimes interrupted.

The history of human civilization therefore rests on a dialectical unity between the achievements of different peoples. All peoples pass through broadly similar stages of history in different parts of the world, but each passes through them in its own particular way.
If we do speak of several distinct civilizations, their differences must still be understood within this larger dialectical unity.

For this reason, we can see a kind of horizontal interaction running through their histories. A later civilization does not simply erase or cancel the civilization that came before it. On the contrary, it carries parts of it forward.

It does this by entering into contact with the earlier civilization, adapting some of its elements to its own conditions, developing others further, and abandoning still others as new and more advanced elements appear.

The general course of human civilization therefore continues to move forward. It does so despite its many twists and turns, and even despite periods of interruption. Those interruptions themselves become part of the larger movement.
If we look specifically at the history of philosophy across the world’s different cultures and civilizations, the same point becomes even clearer.

Even if we accepted the idea of a “closed” civilization or culture, we would still have to admit that philosophy has never developed through internal conditions alone. External conditions have always played a part as well.
But there is an important objective law that we must keep in mind here.

External influences can only take effect through internal conditions. They have to become part of those internal conditions rather than remaining separate from them. Otherwise, their influence will be artificial, superficial, or temporary.
There is another objective law that also matters when we study the relationship between cultures, and especially between philosophical traditions.
The degree of outside influence depends partly on how similar the social and intellectual conditions are in the two countries concerned—the country influencing and the country being influenced.

The closer their conditions are, the stronger the influence is likely to be. But we must look at the right kinds of similarities: the level of scientific development, class relations, and relations of production.
Second: the relative independence of philosophy
To understand the historical setting properly, we also have to take account of another factor: philosophy has a certain relative independence.
This independence appears in several ways. The one that concerns us here is simple.
Every new generation enters a world in which material and social relationships already exist. Those relationships were formed before that generation appeared and independently of its wishes.
The same is true of ideas.

Every generation also inherits a body of ideologies and intellectual traditions that developed before it. It receives a certain amount of intellectual material created by earlier generations, independently of what the new generation itself wants or does.
